opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot. The way I see it, language and perception aren't really competing, but they play different roles. A lot of what we know about the world, especially as kids, we learn without language at all. We watch things fall, we push things around, we see how people move, and we build up this intuitive model of physics and cause and effect long before we can talk about it. That's really the motivation behind JEPA: learning a predictive model of the world from raw sensory data, but predicting in an abstract representation space rather than trying to reconstruct every pixel. You don't need to predict the exact texture of every leaf on a tree to understand that the branch is going to sway in the wind.

So where does language come in? I think of language as a very efficient interface on top of that grounded representation. Once you have a good model of how the world works, language becomes a way to query it, to condition it, to communicate goals, and to transfer knowledge that would be really expensive to discover through experience alone. Someone can tell you "the stove is hot" and you don't have to learn that the hard way.

In practice, what we've seen is that if you first train the visual or video encoder in a self-supervised way, just from observation, and then align it with a language model afterwards, you get representations that are much better at things like understanding motion, temporal dynamics, and physical interactions, compared to models where language supervision is baked in from the start. Language-supervised models tend to pick up whatever is easy to describe in a caption, which is often the static stuff: what objects are in the scene. The things that are hard to put into words, like the subtle way something deforms or how an action unfolds over time, they tend to get underweighted.

So my view is that language should be grounded in the world model rather than the world model being derived from language. You want the foundation to come from perception and prediction, and then language sits on top as this powerful tool for reasoning, planning, and communicating. And I think the really exciting direction is when you combine those, where you can give an agent a goal in language, and it uses its learned world model to imagine the consequences of different actions and plan in that latent space. That's where I think the two really come together.

r001.rationale: It says children build intuitive models of physics and cause and effect by watching and interacting with the world long before they can talk.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting in an abstract representation space instead of reconstructing pixels, but does not say the encoder discards information that is not predictable.

r003.rationale: It proposes giving an agent a language goal and using its world model to imagine action consequences, but does not clearly say that actions encoded in language condition predictions about the future.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, language is incredibly useful, but it's not where the world model lives. If you look at how humans develop, kids build up a pretty sophisticated understanding of the physical world, object permanence, intuitive physics, how things move and interact, long before they can speak. Language comes later and sort of sits on top of that. So in the JEPA view, the core representation is learned from perception, from video, from interaction, by predicting in an abstract latent space rather than predicting pixels. That latent space is where you want the model to capture what's predictable about the world and discard the noise.

Language then plays a few roles. One is as an interface. It's how you specify a goal, ask a question, or communicate a plan. If I have a world model that understands how the environment evolves, I still need some way to tell it what I care about, and language is a very compressed, efficient way to do that. The second role is as a source of knowledge. There's an enormous amount of information encoded in text that you'd never recover from watching video alone, abstract concepts, history, facts about things you can't observe directly. So you'd want to ground language into the perceptual representation, align the two spaces, so that a word like "fragile" actually connects to something about how objects behave when they fall.

What I don't think works well is the reverse, where you try to make language the substrate and bolt perception on as an afterthought. Text is a very lossy description of the world. It leaves out most of what's actually happening in a scene because humans don't bother writing it down. So if your model's internal representation is fundamentally linguistic, you inherit those gaps. Whereas if the representation is grounded in perception and language is attached to it, you get the best of both. You get the richness of what you can observe, and the abstraction and transferability of symbols.

Practically, with things like V-JEPA, we've been focused on getting the perceptual side right first, learning good predictive representations from video without labels. The language integration is something we're actively working on, and the early signals are encouraging, but I'd say the hard problem is still making sure the grounding is real, that the language features are actually tied to the physical structure the model has learned, and not just a correlational shortcut.

r001.rationale: It says children understand physical interactions before speaking and that JEPA learns perceptual representations, but does not clearly state that a model can reason about visual interactions without language.

r002.rationale: It says the latent space captures what is predictable and discards noise, but does not clearly state that JEPA’s encoder discards information specifically because it is not predictable.

r003.rationale: It describes language as a way to specify goals and plans, but does not propose using language-encoded actions to condition predictions about the future.

astra-6.text:
I think language has a really important role to play, but I wouldn’t necessarily make it the foundation of the world model. There’s a lot about the physical world that’s difficult to capture in language. If you watch an object move or interact with something, you’re getting information that would be very cumbersome to describe in words. So we’d like the model to learn directly from those observations, and JEPA is a way of learning to predict in that representation space.

Language can then give us an interface to those representations. You could use it to specify a goal, ask a question about what the model observes, or communicate a prediction. It’s also a source of knowledge that you might never acquire through your own observations.

The interesting research question is how to connect those two things: the representations you learn from perception and the representations you learn from language. Ideally, they complement each other, so you can reason about a situation in a grounded way and use language to guide or express that reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says the model can learn directly from observations, but does not state that it can perform lower-level reasoning about visual interactions without language.

r002.rationale: It does not mention JEPA’s encoder discarding information that is not predictable.

r003.rationale: Language is described as a way to specify goals or communicate predictions, but the response does not propose conditioning future predictions on actions encoded in language.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language has a really important role to play, but I don’t think it has to be the foundation of the world model. A lot of our understanding of the physical world comes from perception and interaction, and much of that knowledge is difficult to express in words.

With something like JEPA, the idea is to learn representations that capture predictable structure in the world without having to predict every pixel. Language could then be connected to those representations. It gives us a way to communicate a goal, ask questions about what’s happening, or draw on knowledge that somebody else has described.

So I see them as complementary. The perceptual model provides grounding, and language provides an interface for communicating with that model and potentially guiding its predictions. The interesting research question is how to learn that connection so that the language actually refers to an understanding of the world.

r001.rationale: The response says perception and interaction provide knowledge that can be difficult to express in words, but it does not state that a model can perform lower-level reasoning about visual interactions without language.

r002.rationale: It says JEPA learns representations that capture predictable structure, but does not state that its encoder discards information that is not predictable.

r003.rationale: It says language can communicate goals and potentially guide predictions, but does not specify actions encoded in language conditioning a world model’s predictions about the future.
